beats.title: TREND, ANOMALY, OR NOT ENOUGH?
beats.subtitle: Read the evidence before you name the pattern
say: NARRATOR
Suppose a line jumps. Is the system changing, is one point unusual, or are you missing the context to decide? In this lesson, you will make that call from evidence.

beats.title: A chart is evidence
beats.caption: Not a verdict. Start with context, then inspect the shape.
beats.alt: An analyst workspace with a large monitor showing five steadily rising weekly points.
say: NARRATOR
Start with context, not shape. A defensible reading begins by asking what was measured, over what period, and on which scale.

beats.title: Inspect context before the line
beats.alt: A weekly checkout error-rate dashboard with title, percent scale, and date axis highlighted in sequence.
say: NARRATOR

Let's inspect this fictional dashboard. First, the title: checkout error rate. Next, the vertical axis and units: percent of sessions. Then the horizontal axis: five weekly observations. Finally, check the visible scale before judging the size of the jump.

beats.title: A reusable four-move routine

steps.title: Context
steps.detail: Read title, axes, units, and time span.

steps.title: Justify
steps.detail: Name the visible cue and qualify the claim.

beats.alt: Four ordered moves: context, pattern, classify, and justify.
say: NARRATOR
Use four moves every time: establish context, inspect the pattern across observations, choose trend, anomaly, or insufficient evidence, then justify that category with a visible cue.

beats.prompt: A line rises sharply, but the chart has no title or units. Which category is defensible?
beats.instructions: Choose a category and name the missing evidence.
beats.model_answer: Insufficient evidence. The title and units are missing, so the line shape has no interpretable meaning.
beats.feedback: The same shape could represent dollars, seconds, or defects. Missing context changes the claim you can defend.
beats.alt: A context-check prompt asking about an unlabeled rising line.

beats.title: DISTINGUISH THE PATTERNS
beats.subtitle: Persistence · departure · missing evidence
say: NARRATOR
With context established, the decision turns on what happens across observations.

beats.title: The decision boundary

left.title: TREND
left.body: A direction persists across multiple observations. It may rise or fall.
left.label: LOOK FOR REPEATED DIRECTION

right.title: ANOMALY
right.body: An observation or compact cluster departs from the surrounding pattern.
right.label: LOOK FOR DEPARTURE FROM CONTEXT

beats.alt: Trend and anomaly compared by persistence versus departure from the surrounding pattern.
say: NARRATOR
A trend sustains a direction across multiple observations. An anomaly departs from what surrounds it. A point's absolute height is less informative than its relationship to several neighbors.

beats.title: A jump followed by a return
beats.insight: The surrounding observations stay near two percent.
beats.alt: Four weekly values near two percent with one isolated spike above seven percent in week three.
say: NARRATOR
Here, week three jumps, then the series returns to its earlier range. That visible return supports anomaly, not a sustained upward trend.

beats.title: Model the classification
beats.problem: Does the week-three spike establish a rising trend?

steps.title: Check context
steps.detail: Weekly checkout error rate, measured as a percentage.

steps.title: Inspect observations
steps.detail: Weeks one, two, four, and five remain near two percent.

steps.title: Classify
steps.detail: One point departs and the series returns to its prior range.

steps.title: Qualify
steps.detail: Investigate the anomaly; do not claim a continuing rise.

beats.alt: A four-step worked example classifying one spike among otherwise stable observations.
say: NARRATOR
An expert does not name the tallest point and stop. They verify the metric, inspect both sides of the spike, classify the departure, and qualify the next action.

beats.prompt: Values are 41, 42, 71, 43, and 44. Trend, anomaly, or insufficient evidence?
beats.instructions: Use the relationship among observations, not the largest number alone.
beats.model_answer: Anomaly. Seventy-one departs sharply, while the next value returns near the earlier range.
beats.feedback: The return toward forty-three separates this from a sustained rise.
beats.alt: A guided classification prompt using five numeric observations.
Five weekly completion-rate points appear progressively, each above the previous point.
say: NARRATOR
Now watch a trend form. No single point does the work. Each new observation extends the same direction, so persistence becomes visible across time.

beats.prompt: A labeled metric moves 68, 61, 55, 47, then 39. Classify the pattern and cite the cue.
beats.instructions: Answer in one sentence before the reveal.
beats.model_answer: A downward trend: the value falls in the same direction across five observations.
beats.feedback: Trend describes persistence, not whether the direction is good, bad, rising, or falling.
beats.alt: An independent prompt with five consecutively decreasing values.

beats.title: Sequence suggests a question, not a cause

events.label: Investigate
events.note: Test alternatives; do not assume cause.

beats.alt: A software release precedes an error increase by eight minutes, followed by investigation.
say: NARRATOR

In this fictional scenario, the release and error spike are close in time. Timing alone makes the release a useful hypothesis, not proof of cause. Logs, traffic, and competing explanations remain to be tested.

beats.title: Transfer: a different domain, same reasoning
beats.insight: Wait time rises across every observed day.
beats.alt: Hospital wait time rises from eighteen to thirty-eight minutes across five weekdays.
say: NARRATOR
Change the domain. Consider a fictional hospital case: wait time rises across five days. The pattern is visible, but the preceding scheduling change still does not prove what caused the rise.

beats.prompt: Wait time rises 18, 22, 27, 32, 38 minutes after a schedule change. Classify and justify.
beats.instructions: Name the pattern, cite one cue, and qualify the causal claim.
beats.model_answer: An upward trend: all five observations rise. The schedule change is a hypothesis, not proof of cause.
beats.feedback: The repeated direction supports trend. Temporal proximity can guide investigation, but causation needs additional evidence.
beats.alt: A transfer prompt combining a five-day wait-time sequence with a nearby schedule change.

beats.q: A data point stands well above its neighbors, then the series returns to its earlier range. Which conclusion is defensible?
options: A sustained upward trend is proven
The spike is an anomaly worth investigating
The nearest event definitely caused it
The series is a downward trend because it falls after the spike
beats.why: One departure can justify investigation, but it does not establish persistence or cause.
beats.alt: A four-option knowledge check about the defensible conclusion after one isolated spike.
say: NARRATOR
One final decision. Commit to the strongest conclusion the evidence supports.

beats.title: Context · Pattern · Classify · Justify
bullets: Read labels, units, time span, and scale
Look across observations, not at one point
Name trend, anomaly, or insufficient evidence
Cite a visible cue and qualify causal claims
beats.note: The quality of the decision lives in the evidence.
beats.alt: A four-step summary of the chart-classification routine.
say: NARRATOR
Run the routine: establish context, inspect across observations, choose the defensible category, and justify it without claiming more than the evidence can support.
